_comment: ASD-STE100 Issue 9 (2025-01-15) vocabulary and rule rulings. Rebuilt from the official PDF, not from a paraphrase of it: the dictionary table (Part 2) was parsed programmatically with pdftotext -layout and every claim in this file that cites a rule number or a dictionary ruling was checked back against the extracted text before being kept. See ste_dictionary_full.json in this same folder for the full ~2060-entry parsed dictionary (of 2149 the standard states it carries: 875 approved, 1274 not approved) and SOURCING.md for what changed from the previous hand-written version and why.

modal_notes._comment: Rule 3.2 gives 6 approved verb forms/tenses; CAN, WILL and MUST are the only approved modal auxiliaries and each carries its own dictionary entry.
modal_notes.can: CAN (v). Dictionary entry lists its own forms as 'CAN, CAN, COULD -- No other verb forms', but the same entry then says explicitly: 'Do not use COULD (v) to show possibility.' Treat COULD as banned in practice despite being grouped in CAN's paradigm.
modal_notes.cannot: CANNOT (v) is its own approved dictionary entry, the negative of CAN, meaning 'to not be able to.' Write it as one word.
modal_notes.will: WILL (v). Dictionary entry: 'No other verb forms.' Simple future only.
modal_notes.must: MUST (v). Dictionary entry: 'Auxiliary modal verb that shows obligation.'

banned_modal_replacements._comment: Word-for-word dictionary rulings, verified against Issue 9 Part 2. 'might' has no dictionary entry at all -- it is banned only by the general rule that an unlisted word is not approved, not by an explicit ruling.
banned_modal_replacements.could: can -- STE explicitly bans COULD for showing possibility even though it is listed under CAN's own verb-form group
banned_modal_replacements.might: not in the Issue 9 dictionary at all; there is no official ruling to cite, restructure the sentence around must/can/will

verb_forms_allowed._comment: Rule 3.2, the complete list. Nothing outside these six is approved, whatever the verb.
forms: the past participle form, used as an adjective only

verb_construction_bans._comment: Rule 3.4. Two distinct failure shapes, both auxiliary-verb constructions.

perfect_tense.non_ste: The operator has adjusted the linkage.

passive_auxiliary.pattern: is to be / can be / must be / will be + past participle

examples.non_ste: The seat is to be installed before you install the cushion.
examples.ste: Before you install the cushion, install the seat.

examples.non_ste: The volume control can be adjusted.
examples.ste: You can adjust the volume control.

examples.non_ste: The sleeve will be adjusted by the robot.
examples.ste: The robot will adjust the sleeve.

approved_verb_replacements._comment: All four verified as 'MAKE SURE (v)' in the Part 2 dictionary body (check: line ~8143, verify: ~19365, confirm: ~8625, ensure: ~10293 of the -layout extraction). MAKE SURE is a two-word approved verb, its approved meaning is 'to verify and/or do the necessary steps.'

examples: make sure that it is safe to continue
make sure that the tightness is correct
make sure that the ground run is done
make sure that the correct value is used

phrasal_verbs._comment: REPLACES a previous version of this file that shipped ~555 generic English phrasal-verb entries (e.g. 'zone out', 'wedge in', 'trickle down') with invented replacements. None of those exist anywhere in the Issue 9 dictionary; they read as a pasted-in general-English resource, not an STE ruling. The standard does not carry a phrasal-verb lookup table at all -- Rule 9.3 states this outright: 'You will not usually find phrasal verbs listed as not approved in the dictionary.' What follows is the actual rule and its own worked examples.
phrasal_verbs.principle: Do not combine two approved words to make a new phrase (a phrasal verb) whose meaning differs from the approved meanings of its parts. This is a productive-grammar ban, not a word list: any two approved words can accidentally form a banned phrasal verb.

worked_examples.note: 'put' and 'out' are both approved words, but 'put out' meaning 'extinguish' is not one of their approved meanings.
'give' and 'off' are both approved, 'give off' is not.

approved_exceptions._comment: Rule 9.3: 'Only a small number of phrasal verbs (for example, put on and come on) are approved in the dictionary. They all have a restricted meaning.' These are dictionary headwords in their own right, verified against Part 2.
approved_exceptions.PUT ON: to cover your skin, or other items that give protection, with clothing or equipment (restricted to this sense only)
approved_exceptions.COME ON: to become bright, said of a light or indicator (restricted to this sense only)
approved_exceptions.GO OFF: to become dark, said of a light or indicator when its power source is removed (restricted to this sense only)

banned_words_software._comment: Software-specific words the general dictionary bans, each verified against Part 2. Where a word is also listed as a Rule 1.12 technical verb, both facts are given: they are not a contradiction, they are a priority order.

delete.note: Part 2: 'delete (v)' is NOT approved; alternatives are ERASE (v) or REMOVE (v). But Rule 1.12's 'Computer processes and applications' category lists 'delete' by name as an example UI/application technical verb. Rule 1.12 itself resolves the tension: 'If there is an approved verb in the dictionary that accurately gives the instruction..., use the approved verb. Do not use a technical verb if it is possible to write the same sentence with the words... that are approved in the dictionary.' So erase/remove take priority; delete is a fallback for when neither fits.

destroy.note: Part 2: 'destroy (v)' -> BREAK (v). (An earlier revision used UNSERVICEABLE (adj) as the approved alternative; the revision-history table records that it 'was removed as the approved alternative' in this issue.)

drop.note: Part 2: 'drop (v)' -> FALL (v) for the physical-motion sense. Not evaluated for the general-English 'decrease' sense used elsewhere in this file's recurring_errors.

issue.note: 'issue' as a noun for 'problem' has no dictionary entry at all, approved or banned. Use 'problem' or 'error', both of which are ordinary approved nouns.

technical_verb_categories._comment: Rule 1.12, verbatim category 2 ('Computer processes and applications'), the only part of the technical-verb list that is software-specific. The dictionary itself carries none of these -- Rule 1.12 exists precisely because 'the dictionary does not include technical verbs, there are too many, and each subject field uses different technical verbs.' A technical verb may be used ONLY when no approved dictionary verb already covers the same instruction (see the 'delete' entry above for the resolution order), and must still obey every other verb rule (section 3: six forms only, active voice, etc).

recurring_errors._comment: Every entry here is a verified Part 2 dictionary ruling for the exact word, not a paraphrase of general STE advice. Word senses that split into more than one approved alternative keep all of them rather than picking one.
recurring_errors.since_as_conjunction: because -- Part 2: SINCE (conj) is approved for its time sense ('from some time in the past until now'); for the causal sense ('because') it is not approved and the dictionary gives BECAUSE (conj) as the alternative.
recurring_errors.any: delete or restructure -- Part 2: 'any (adj)' is not approved; its own dictionary note reads 'Frequently, an alternative for this word is not necessary.' 'any (pron)' is a separate entry, approved alternative ONE (TN).
recurring_errors.now: delete or 'at this time' -- Part 2: 'now (adv)' -> AT THIS TIME
recurring_errors.need_to: restructure into the imperative -- 'need to' has no dictionary entry; 'need (v)' alone is not approved, alternative NECESSARY (adj) ('It is necessary that...'). Rule 5.3 requires the imperative form in procedures regardless.
recurring_errors.have_to: restructure into the imperative -- Part 2: 'have to (v)' is not approved; its own note reads 'Use a verb in the imperative form.' (An earlier revision listed MUST (v) as the alternative; the revision-history table records it was removed in this issue.)
recurring_errors.insert: put -- Part 2: 'insert (v)' -> PUT (v) or, for a fitted/engaged sense, ENGAGE (v). (SQL INSERT stays as quoted syntax, outside STE's scope.)
recurring_errors.repeat: do again -- Part 2: 'repeat (v)' -> AGAIN (adv), used as 'do... again'
recurring_errors.acceptable: permitted -- give the limit -- Part 2: 'acceptable (adj)' -> PERMITTED (adj)
recurring_errors.complete_adjective: full, all, or completed, depending on sense -- Part 2's 'complete (adj)' entry gives three separate approved alternatives for three separate senses: FULL (adj) ('three complete cycles' -> 'three full cycles'), ALL (adj) ('the complete test results' -> 'all the test results'), COMPLETED (adj) (state/status sense). Pick the alternative that matches the sense in play, do not default to 'completed.'
recurring_errors.the_example_below: name the target or put the reference after -- not a single-word dictionary ruling; follows from Rule 8.3's parenthetical-reference pattern ('refer to paragraphs 2 thru 5') rather than a forward 'below' pointer.

punctuation_and_word_count._comment: Section 8 (Punctuation and word count) plus the two sentence-length caps from sections 5 and 6, and the contraction ban from section 4. All verified against the extracted rule text.

no_semicolon.note: All standard English punctuation is allowed except the semicolon. Split into two sentences instead.

hyphens_for_directly_related_words.note: Connect compound adjectives, two-word fractions/numbers, letter/number-plus-noun shape terms, compound verbs, and vowel-ending-prefix constructions.

parentheses_uses.note: Seven permitted uses: illustration/text references, item numbers/letters, procedure step numbers, abbreviations, singular/plural pairs, brief explanations, alternatives.

vertical_list_colon_word_count.note: A colon before a vertical list counts as a period: everything before it must obey the applicable sentence-length cap (20 words procedural / 25 descriptive), and each item after it is its own sentence subject to the same cap.

parenthetical_text_counts_as_one_word.note: Parenthetical text (including identifiers and abbreviations) counts as exactly one word of the sentence it sits in, but the words inside the parentheses form their own separate sentence for counting purposes if they are a full clause.

elements_counted_as_one_word.note: Numbers, numbers with units, and abbreviations each count as one word.

hyphenated_words_count_as_one_word.note: A hyphenated adjective group before a noun (e.g. 'soap-and-water solution') counts as one word for the sentence-length caps.

no_contractions.note: Write all words in full (no 'don't', 'isn't', 'aren't'), and never omit nouns, verbs, subjects, or articles to shorten a sentence.

extracted_and_verified_in_this_pass.note: See ste_dictionary_full.json in this folder for the full parsed table (2062 of 2149 entries recovered by the automated pdftotext -layout parser; the gap is documented there as a known extraction limitation, not a claim that the missing ~4% don't exist).

ai_slop._comment: AI-overused words not in the ASD dictionary and not covered by Issue 9 at all -- this section is deliberately outside the standard, unchanged from the previous version. Source: AminBlg/SimpleEnglish word-swaps.md. If a word carries no fact, delete it instead of replacing it.
ai_slop.robust: delete or give the measurable property
ai_slop.powerful: delete or give the measurable property
ai_slop.comprehensive: delete or give the measurable property
ai_slop.performant: delete or give the measurable property
ai_slop.is_designed_to: delete -- say what it does instead
ai_slop.aims_to: delete -- say what it does instead
ai_slop.etc: name the items or write 'and more'
ai_slop.gracefully_handles: delete -- say what it does (e.g. 'retries three times, then stops')
ai_slop.addresses_the_issue: corrects the fault or removes the error
ai_slop.tackles: corrects the fault or removes the error
ai_slop.and/or: pick one, or write 'X, or Y, or both'
